study.title: Who Is the World?
study.focus: How wide is God's love, and how do the teachers read 'the world' and 'whoever believes'?
study.take: This take lets the teachers disagree in the open: Henry and Calvin read the offer as going out to all; Gill reads 'the world' as the elect among every nation. Augustine and Calvin keep the human side in view.
study.closing: Whatever you decide about the width of God's love, what does the invitation to whoever believes ask of you?

scripture.16: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.
scripture.17: For God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him.
scripture.18: He who believes in him is not judged. He who doesn’t believe has been judged already, because he has not believed in the name of the only born Son of God.

verse_questions.17: Saved: everyone, or those who believe?
verse_questions.18: Who is safe, and who is not?

summaries.MHC3.16.06: Matthew Henry says that even though many in the world perish, God giving his only Son was still love for the whole world, because through him a general offer of life and salvation goes out to all. He compares it to announcing a pardon to a rebellious province: it is love to invite everyone to come in, plead for it on their knees, and return to their loyalty.
summaries.GIL3.16.01: John Gill says the world here does not mean every single person. The special love of God shown in giving his Son is not for everyone, he argues, because Christ is not given to every person: whoever receives the Son also receives all things freely with him, and that is not true of every man.
summaries.CAL3.16.08: John Calvin says the word only-begotten is emphatic, meant to magnify the warmth of God's love for us. Since people are not easily convinced that God loves them, John states plainly that we are so dear to God that he did not spare even his only Son for our sake. Calvin concludes that anyone who is not satisfied with this proof and still doubts insults Christ, as if he were an ordinary man handed over to death at random.
summaries.CAL3.16.09: John Calvin says we should rather consider that the more God values his only Son, the more precious our salvation was to him, since he chose that this Son should die to pay for it. Christ is the only Son by nature, and he shares that honor with us by adoption when we are joined to his body.
summaries.CAL3.16.10: John Calvin calls it a remarkable tribute to faith that it frees us from everlasting destruction. Although we seem born to death, faith in Christ offers certain deliverance, so we need not fear the death that hangs over us. He says the word whosoever invites everyone to share in life and takes away every excuse from unbelievers.
summaries.CAL3.16.11: John Calvin says that although nothing in the world deserves God's favor, God shows he is reconciled to the whole world by inviting all people without exception to faith in Christ, which is the way into life. He adds a reminder: life is promised to everyone who believes, but faith is not common to all.
summaries.CAL3.17.02: John Calvin says John repeats the word world so that no one who keeps to the road of faith will think himself shut out. Calvin reads judge here as condemn, and says this shows the real purpose of Christ's coming: there was no need for him to come to destroy people who were already ruined.
summaries.GIL3.17.03: John Gill reads the world that is saved as the world of the elect in general: those God decided to save and chose to receive salvation through Jesus Christ. Christ was appointed to be their salvation and came to seek and save them, especially his chosen people among the Gentiles. That is why he is called God's salvation to the ends of the earth, and everyone everywhere is called to look to him and be saved.
summaries.AUG3.17-18.1.01: Augustine says that, as far as it is up to the physician, Christ came to heal the sick, and a patient who will not follow the physician's orders destroys himself. Christ is called the Saviour of the world because he came to save the world, not to judge it; the one who refuses to be saved by him is judged by himself.
summaries.GIL3.18.02: John Gill says the believer, Jew or Gentile, faces no condemnation because he is in Christ. The sentence of death passed on all in Adam, but Christ, standing in for his people, suffered that death in their place, so his death shields them from all condemnation and from the curse of the law. Having passed from death to life, they will never enter into condemnation.
summaries.CAL3.18.02: John Calvin says the words is not condemned mean that believers are safe from the fear of condemnation. For everyone who rejects the life given in Christ, nothing remains but death, since life consists in nothing else than faith.
summaries.JFB3.18.01: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown say the believer has passed from death to life the moment he believes. The one who is condemned already is the one who rejects the single way out that God gave his Son to provide, and so chooses to stay condemned.

labels.jewish_source: A later Jewish writing that Gill cites; not a statement of what people believed in Jesus's day.
